title: Saha navavatu: a prayer for us both
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: a father sends his son back again and again, and a chant for teacher and student
carry: the teacher prays with the student, not above
tomorrow: why say peace three times, and not just once?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma ended its week in honey: everything feeds and is fed. The four great sayings are done. Now, the chants that stand around the texts.

In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, Varuna, and says: sir, teach me Brahman. Varuna gives him a few pointers and sends him off to find it by tapas, hard inner effort. Bhrigu comes back: it's food. Seek again by tapas, says his father. Breath. Seek again. Mind. Again. Understanding. Again. Four times he returns, and four times the answer is the same, patient and unhurried. And the fifth time, Bhrigu understands: Brahman is bliss.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `SEEK AGAIN. AND AGAIN.` → `BRAHMAN IS BLISS.`

segments.voice: The same Upanishad gives teacher and student a peace chant to say together before study, known by its first words, saha navavatu. Tradition chants it with the Katha too, and every peace chant closes the same way: Om, shanti, shanti, shanti. Here's what it asks, in plain words. May it protect us both. May it nourish us both. May we work together with strength. May our study be full of light. May we not turn against each other. Notice the word both. The teacher doesn't stand outside the prayer, handing it down. The teacher needs protecting and feeding too. And notice the last request. Of everything that could go wrong in a hard lesson, the chant names this one: that the two people in the room would come to resent each other. A question pushes, an answer stings, and a little bitterness creeps in. Many teachers read Varuna as that prayer lived out: four times he sends his son back, and never once sends him away. This is how Hindu tradition holds learning: guru and student under one prayer, a bond, not a transaction. So before the text even opens, the chant asks for what the text can't supply: two people still on the same side when the lesson ends.
screen: `SAHA NAVAVATU: US BOTH.` · `MAY WE NOT TURN AGAINST EACH OTHER.` · `BHRIGU, SENT BACK, NEVER AWAY.` · then, large: `GURU AND STUDENT, ONE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you chant, say saha navavatu slowly, all the way to the three shantis, holding in mind someone you learn from and someone who learns from you. If you don't pray, write those two names side by side on one line, and look at them together for the rest of the sit: both under one prayer.
The peace chants: lines said before and after the study of an Upanishad, each ending in shanti, peace, three times. Saha navavatu asks for teacher and student both.
Pocket this: the teacher prays with the student, not above. Saha navavatu: protect us both. See you tomorrow.
